key_terms.meaning: X[k] = Σ<sub>n=0</sub><sup>N−1</sup> x[n] e<sup>−j2πkn/N</sup>, with 1/N in the synthesis sum; books that put 1/N in the analysis sum write a<sub>k</sub> = X[k]/N
A sequence with x[n] = x[n+N] for all n; the smallest such N is the fundamental period
Which multiple of the fundamental frequency 2π/N a DTFS term sits at; for a period-N sequence only N distinct values of k exist
X(e<sup>jω</sup>) = Σₙ x[n] e<sup>−jωn</sup>; the continuous, 2π-periodic spectrum of an aperiodic sequence
X(e<sup>j(ω+2π)</sup>) = X(e<sup>jω</sup>) because e<sup>−j2πn</sup> = 1 for integer n; the spectrum repeats every 2π rad/sample
Σₙ |x[n]| < ∞; a sufficient condition for the DTFT to exist and be continuous
X[k] = Σₙ₌₀<sup>N−1</sup> x[n] W<sub>N</sub><sup>nk</sup>, k = 0, …, N−1; N samples of the DTFT at ω = 2πk/N
W<sub>N</sub> = e<sup>−j2π/N</sup>, so W<sub>N</sub><sup>nk</sup> = e<sup>−j2πnk/N</sup>; the fixed complex number that makes the DFT a matrix product
X(z) = Σₙ₌₋∞<sup>∞</sup> x[n] z<sup>−n</sup>, a power series in z⁻¹ evaluated at a complex number z
The set of z values for which the z-transform sum converges absolutely; it is part of the transform, not an optional extra
Putting z on the unit circle turns X(z) into the DTFT; the DTFT is the z-transform evaluated on |z| = 1 when the ROC includes the unit circle
x[n − n₀] ↔ z<sup>−n₀</sup> X(z); the ROC is unchanged except that z = 0 or z = ∞ may be added or removed
x[n] * h[n] ↔ X(z)H(z); the ROC of the product contains the intersection of the two ROCs
aⁿ x[n] ↔ X(z/a); the ROC radii scale by |a|, and a pole at p moves to a·p
Writing X(z)/z as a sum of simple terms whose inverse transforms are known geometric sequences
Dividing numerator by denominator to get a series in z⁻¹ or z; the coefficients of the series are the sequence values
A sequence that is zero for n < n₀; its ROC is the region outside the outermost pole, and z = ∞ may be included
H(z) = Y(z)/X(z), the z-transform of the impulse response of an LTI system
Values of z where H(z) → ∞ (roots of the denominator) and where H(z) = 0 (roots of the numerator)
A causal LTI system is stable exactly when all poles of H(z) lie strictly inside the unit circle |z| = 1
H(z) evaluated at z = e<sup>jω</sup>; valid only when the ROC contains the unit circle

takeaways: A period-N sequence carries only N independent complex exponentials, so its DTFS has exactly N distinct coefficients and then repeats.
The DTFT is continuous in ω but always periodic with period 2π, because discrete time makes frequency a wrapped, circular quantity.
The N-point DFT is just the DTFT sampled at ω = 2πk/N, which is why it can be computed as a finite N × N matrix product.
The z-transform is a power series; the algebraic formula alone is incomplete, and the ROC is what pins down the sequence.
Every operation you do in time — shift, scale, convolve, difference — has a one-line z-domain counterpart with a predictable effect on the ROC.
Inverse z-transform is two steps: invert the algebra, then use the ROC to choose causal or anti-causal terms for each pole.
The poles of H(z) relative to the unit circle decide stability and shape the frequency response, without ever solving the difference equation in time.
A causal system is stable only if every pole is strictly inside |z| = 1; a single pole on or outside the circle breaks it.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the DTFS and DTFT definitions with their properties, the z-transform with its ROC and properties, and the analysis of a difference-equation system: H(z), poles and zeros, h[n], causality and stability. A long answer earns its marks with the ROC drawn next to the poles and every number worked to the end.

bank.q: Define the discrete-time Fourier series of a period-N sequence. Write the analysis and synthesis equations, show that the coefficients X[k] repeat with period N, and verify the pair on one period of 1, 1, 0, 0.
outline: Periodic sequence x[n + N] = x[n]; harmonics e<sup>j2πkn/N</sup>
Analysis X[k] = Σ<sub>n=0</sub><sup>N−1</sup> x[n] e<sup>−j2πkn/N</sup>; synthesis x[n] = (1/N) Σ<sub>k=0</sub><sup>N−1</sup> X[k] e<sup>j2πkn/N</sup>
Only N distinct harmonics, so X[k + N] = X[k]
Line spectrum at Ω<sub>k</sub> = 2πk/N
Worked check with numbers
answer: A sequence is periodic with period N when x[n + N] = x[n] for every integer n. N is the smallest such positive integer, counted in samples.
The harmonics are the complex exponentials e<sup>j2πkn/N</sup>. Harmonic k makes k full cycles across one period, so its frequency is Ω<sub>k</sub> = 2πk/N radians per sample.
The DTFS pair used in this book puts 1/N in the synthesis sum. Analysis: X[k] = Σn=0N−1 x[n] e−j2πkn/N. Synthesis: x[n] = (1/N) Σk=0N−1 X[k] ej2πkn/N.

Why the pair closes: put the synthesis sum into the analysis sum. The inner sum Σ<sub>n=0</sub><sup>N−1</sup> e<sup>j2π(m−k)n/N</sup> is a geometric series that equals N when m = k and 0 otherwise. So the right-hand side becomes (1/N)·N·X[k] = X[k]. This orthogonality of the N harmonics is what makes the coefficients unique.

Periodicity of the coefficients: replace k by k + N. The exponent gains e<sup>−j2πNn/N</sup> = e<sup>−j2πn</sup> = 1 for every integer n, so X[k + N] = X[k]. Harmonic k + N is the same sequence as harmonic k; only N distinct harmonics exist, unlike the continuous-time Fourier series, which has infinitely many.

For real x[n], X[N − k] = X*[k]: the magnitude spectrum is even and the phase is odd about k = N/2. Many books write a<sub>k</sub> = X[k]/N (1/N in analysis); the sequence x[n] is the same either way, so state the convention first.

answer.text: Check on N = 4 with one period x = [1, 1, 0, 0]. Only n = 0 and n = 1 contribute, so X[k] = 1 + e<sup>−jπk/2</sup>.

answer: Conjugate check: X[3] = 1 + j = X*[1], as the real-signal rule says.

Synthesis check at n = 0: x[0] = (1/4)(2 + (1 − j) + 0 + (1 + j)) = (1/4)(4) = 1. At n = 2 the factors e<sup>jπk</sup> are 1, −1, 1, −1, so x[2] = (1/4)(2 − (1 − j) + 0 − (1 + j)) = (1/4)(0) = 0. Both match the given samples.
Line spectrum: the four values sit at Ω = 0, π/2, π and 3π/2 rad/sample, and the pattern 2, 1 − j, 0, 1 + j repeats for k = 4 to 7, 8 to 11, and so on.

bank.q: Show that the DTFT of any sequence is periodic in ω with period 2π rad/sample. State a sufficient condition for the DTFT to exist, check it for (0.8)ⁿu[n], and give sequences for which the ordinary DTFT fails.
outline: Substitute ω + 2π into the defining sum
Use e<sup>−j2πn</sup> = 1 for integer n
Sufficient condition: Σ|x[n]| < ∞
Check (0.8)ⁿu[n]: sum 5, X(e<sup>j0</sup>) = 5
u[n] needs impulses; 2ⁿu[n] has no DTFT
answer: Definition, with ω in radians per sample: X(ejω) = Σn=−∞∞ x[n] e−jωn.
Replace ω by ω + 2π. Each term becomes x[n] e<sup>−jωn</sup> e<sup>−j2πn</sup>.
For every integer n, e<sup>−j2πn</sup> = cos(2πn) − j sin(2πn) = 1. So every term is unchanged and X(e<sup>j(ω+2π)</sup>) = X(e<sup>jω</sup>).

The periodicity comes from discrete time, not from the signal: x[n] need not repeat at all. One period, −π < ω ≤ π, carries the whole spectrum, and ω = π is the highest frequency a sampled sequence can show.

Existence: if x[n] is absolutely summable, Σ|x[n]| < ∞, then |X(e<sup>jω</sup>)| ≤ Σ|x[n]| for every ω. The sum converges uniformly and X is a continuous function of ω. This condition is sufficient, not necessary: finite-energy sequences such as sin(ω<sub>c</sub>n)/(πn) have a DTFT in the mean-square sense.
Check for x[n] = (0.8)ⁿu[n]: Σ|x[n]| = 1 + 0.8 + 0.64 + … = 1/(1 − 0.8) = 5, which is finite. The DTFT is the geometric sum 1/(1 − 0.8e<sup>−jω</sup>).

answer.text: Values of that DTFT, showing the 2π repeat:

head: ω
1 − 0.8 cos ω (real part of the denominator)
|X(e<sup>jω</sup>)|

answer: Failure 1, the unit step: Σ u[n] = 1 + 1 + 1 + … diverges. The fraction 1/(1 − e<sup>−jω</sup>) is infinite at ω = 2πk, so the DTFT exists only in the generalised sense, with impulses of area π added there: 1/(1 − e<sup>−jω</sup>) + π Σ<sub>k</sub> δ(ω − 2πk).

Failure 2, a growing sequence: x[n] = 2ⁿu[n] has terms that grow without bound, so no ordinary or generalised DTFT exists. Its z-transform z/(z − 2) still exists for |z| > 2, which does not include the unit circle.

Link to real frequency: ω = ΩT, so one 2π period in ω is one sampling frequency Ωₛ = 2π/T in rad/s. At a sampling rate of 8000 samples/s, ω = π means 4000 Hz and ω = 2π means 8000 Hz, which looks the same as 0 Hz.
Summary: the DTFT always repeats every 2π; it exists as an ordinary continuous function whenever Σ|x[n]| is finite.

bank.q: Define the z-transform of a sequence and its region of convergence. Explain with examples why two different sequences can share the same algebraic X(z), and state the ROC rules for finite-length, right-sided, left-sided and two-sided sequences.
outline: X(z) = Σ x[n] z<sup>−n</sup>, a power series in z<sup>−1</sup>
ROC = set of z where the sum converges absolutely; depends on |z| only, so it is bounded by circles
aⁿu[n] and −aⁿu[−n−1] give the same z/(z − a) with ROCs |z| > |a| and |z| < |a|
Finite-length: whole plane except possibly 0 and ∞; right-sided: outside the outermost pole; left-sided: inside the innermost pole; two-sided: an annulus or nothing
ROC contains no poles and is connected
answer: Definition: for a sequence x[n] and a complex number z, X(z) = Σn=−∞∞ x[n] z−n.

Region of convergence: the set of z for which Σ|x[n]||z|<sup>−n</sup> is finite. Writing z = re<sup>jθ</sup> shows that only r = |z| matters, so the ROC is bounded by circles centred at the origin. It is connected and contains no pole, because the transform is infinite at a pole.
On the unit circle z = e<sup>jω</sup>, X(z) becomes the DTFT, but only when |z| = 1 lies inside the ROC.

Same algebra, two sequences. Right-sided: x₁[n] = (0.8)ⁿu[n] gives Σ<sub>n≥0</sub> (0.8z<sup>−1</sup>)ⁿ = 1/(1 − 0.8z<sup>−1</sup>) = z/(z − 0.8), which converges when |0.8z<sup>−1</sup>| < 1, that is |z| > 0.8.

Left-sided: x₂[n] = −(0.8)ⁿu[−n − 1] = −(0.8)ⁿ for n ≤ −1. Put m = −n: X₂(z) = −Σ<sub>m≥1</sub> (z/0.8)<sup>m</sup> = −(z/0.8)/(1 − z/0.8) = z/(z − 0.8), which converges when |z/0.8| < 1, that is |z| < 0.8.

So z/(z − 0.8) alone does not name a sequence. With |z| > 0.8 it is the decaying causal sequence 1, 0.8, 0.64, …; with |z| < 0.8 it is the anti-causal sequence x₂[−1] = −1.25, x₂[−2] = −1.5625, … Check at z = 1, inside the first ROC: Σ 0.8ⁿ = 5 and 1/(1 − 0.8) = 5.

answer.text: ROC rules, each with an example:

head: Sequence type
ROC
Example and its ROC
rows: whole plane, except z = 0 if n₂ > 0 and z = ∞ if n₁ < 0

answer: Two-sided example in full: x[n] = (1/3)ⁿu[n] − (1/2)ⁿu[−n − 1] has X(z) = z/(z − 1/3) + z/(z − 1/2) = z(2z − 5/6)/[(z − 1/3)(z − 1/2)], poles at 1/3 and 1/2, zeros at 0 and 5/12, ROC 1/3 < |z| < 1/2. The unit circle is outside this ring, so this sequence has no DTFT.
An empty ROC: swap the roles, x[n] = (1/2)ⁿu[n] − (1/3)ⁿu[−n − 1]. The parts need |z| > 1/2 and |z| < 1/3 at the same time, which no z satisfies, so the z-transform does not exist.
Conclusion: always write the ROC with X(z). The poles bound the ROC, the side of the sequence picks which circle, and the unit-circle test tells whether a DTFT exists.

bank.q: State and prove the time-shift, z-domain scaling, convolution and multiplication-by-n properties of the z-transform, give the ROC in each case, and check each on a numerical example built from (0.5)ⁿu[n].
outline: Shift: x[n − n₀] ↔ z<sup>−n₀</sup>X(z), ROC unchanged except possibly z = 0 or ∞
Scaling: aⁿx[n] ↔ X(z/a), ROC radii × |a|
Convolution: x[n] * h[n] ↔ X(z)H(z), ROC contains the intersection
Multiplication by n: n x[n] ↔ −z dX/dz, same ROC
Numerical check of each rule
answer: Base pair: x[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n] ↔ X(z) = z/(z − 0.5) = 1/(1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>), ROC |z| > 0.5. Every proof starts from X(z) = Σ x[n] z<sup>−n</sup>.

Time shift. Proof: Σ x[n − n₀] z<sup>−n</sup>; put m = n − n₀ to get z<sup>−n₀</sup> Σ x[m] z<sup>−m</sup> = z<sup>−n₀</sup>X(z). ROC: unchanged, except that the factor z<sup>−n₀</sup> can remove or add z = 0 or z = ∞. Example: δ[n] ↔ 1 for all z, but δ[n − 1] ↔ z<sup>−1</sup>, which excludes z = 0.

Shift check: y[n] = x[n − 2] = (0.5)<sup>n−2</sup>u[n − 2] ↔ z<sup>−2</sup>·z/(z − 0.5) = z<sup>−1</sup>/(z − 0.5). Its first nonzero sample is y[2] = 1, and long division of z<sup>−1</sup>/(z − 0.5) = z<sup>−2</sup>/(1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>) starts with 1·z<sup>−2</sup>. They agree.
z-domain scaling. Proof: Σ aⁿx[n] z<sup>−n</sup> = Σ x[n](z/a)<sup>−n</sup> = X(z/a). ROC: if X converges for r₁ < |z| < r₂, X(z/a) converges for |a|r₁ < |z| < |a|r₂. A pole at p moves to a·p.
Scaling check: u[n] ↔ z/(z − 1), |z| > 1. With a = 0.5, (0.5)ⁿu[n] ↔ (z/0.5)/(z/0.5 − 1) = z/(z − 0.5), and the ROC |z| > 1 becomes |z| > 0.5. The pole moved from 1 to 0.5, as the rule says.

Convolution. Proof: Σ<sub>n</sub> Σ<sub>k</sub> x[k]h[n − k] z<sup>−n</sup>; put m = n − k so z<sup>−n</sup> = z<sup>−k</sup>z<sup>−m</sup>, and the double sum splits into X(z)·H(z). ROC: contains ROC<sub>x</sub> ∩ ROC<sub>h</sub>, and can be larger if a pole cancels.

answer.text: Convolution check: (0.5)ⁿu[n] * u[n] has transform z²/[(z − 0.5)(z − 1)], ROC |z| > 1. Partial fractions give 2/(1 − z<sup>−1</sup>) − 1/(1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>), so the result is (2 − 0.5ⁿ)u[n]. Direct convolution is the running sum of 0.5ⁿ:

answer: Multiplication by n. Proof: dX/dz = Σ (−n) x[n] z<sup>−n−1</sup>, so −z dX/dz = Σ n x[n] z<sup>−n</sup>. ROC: unchanged, because a power series and its term-by-term derivative converge on the same region.

Multiplication-by-n check: for X = z/(z − 0.5), dX/dz = −0.5/(z − 0.5)², so n(0.5)ⁿu[n] ↔ 0.5z/(z − 0.5)², ROC |z| > 0.5. At z = 2 the formula gives 1/(1.5)² = 0.4444. The defining sum at z = 2 is Σ n(0.5)ⁿ2<sup>−n</sup> = Σ n(0.25)ⁿ = 0.25/(0.75)² = 0.4444. They agree.
Summary: shift multiplies by z<sup>−n₀</sup>, scaling replaces z by z/a, convolution multiplies transforms, and multiplication by n differentiates; the ROC travels with each rule as stated.

bank.q: Compute the 4-point DFT of x[n] = {1, 1, 0, 0}. Then write the DTFT of the same sequence and verify that the four DFT values are samples of it at the correct frequencies.
outline: W₄ = −j and its powers
DTFT X(e<sup>jω</sup>) = 1 + e<sup>−jω</sup> = 2cos(ω/2)e<sup>−jω/2</sup>
Sample at ω = 2πk/4 = 0, π/2, π, 3π/2 and match
answer: Twiddle factor: W₄ = e<sup>−j2π/4</sup> = e<sup>−jπ/2</sup> = −j. Its powers are W₄⁰ = 1, W₄¹ = −j, W₄² = −1, W₄³ = j, and they repeat every 4.

answer.text: DFT: X[k] = Σ<sub>n=0</sub><sup>3</sup> x[n]W₄<sup>nk</sup>. Only x[0] = x[1] = 1 are nonzero, so X[k] = 1 + W₄<sup>k</sup>.
The same result in matrix form, X = W x:

answer: DTFT of the same finite sequence: X(e<sup>jω</sup>) = Σ x[n]e<sup>−jωn</sup> = 1 + e<sup>−jω</sup>. Factor out e<sup>−jω/2</sup>: X(e<sup>jω</sup>) = e<sup>−jω/2</sup>(e<sup>jω/2</sup> + e<sup>−jω/2</sup>) = 2cos(ω/2)e<sup>−jω/2</sup>. So |X(e<sup>jω</sup>)| = 2|cos(ω/2)| and the phase is −ω/2 where the cosine is positive.

answer.text: The N-point DFT samples the DTFT at ω<sub>k</sub> = 2πk/N = 0, π/2, π, 3π/2:

answer: Phase check at k = 1: −ω/2 = −π/4, and ∠(1 − j) = −π/4. At k = 3 the DTFT phase is −3π/4 + π = π/4 (the cosine is negative there, which adds π), and ∠(1 + j) = π/4.
Energy check (Parseval): Σ|x[n]|² = 1 + 1 = 2, and (1/N)Σ|X[k]|² = (1/4)(4 + 2 + 0 + 2) = 2.

Conclusion: the four DFT values are exactly the DTFT at ω = 2πk/4. The DFT shows no more than these four points; zero padding to 8 points would add the DTFT at ω = π/4, 3π/4, … with no new information about x[n].

bank.q: Find the inverse z-transform of X(z) = z/((z − 1/2)(z − 1/3)) for each possible ROC: |z| > 1/2, |z| < 1/3 and 1/3 < |z| < 1/2. Say which result is causal and which is stable.
outline: |z| > 1/2: x[n] = 6[(1/2)ⁿ − (1/3)ⁿ]u[n], causal and stable
|z| < 1/3: x[n] = 6[(1/3)ⁿ − (1/2)ⁿ]u[−n−1], anti-causal, unstable
Only the ROC that contains |z| = 1 gives a stable sequence
Each answer states the ROC
answer: Poles: z = 1/2 and z = 1/3. Possible ROCs are bounded by these circles: |z| > 1/2, 1/3 < |z| < 1/2, and |z| < 1/3.
Multiply back by z: X(z) = 6·z/(z − 1/2) − 6·z/(z − 1/3). Each term has the standard form z/(z − a).
Pairs: z/(z − a) ↔ aⁿu[n] when |z| > |a|, and ↔ −aⁿu[−n−1] when |z| < |a|.
ROC |z| > 1/2: outside both poles, so both terms are right-sided: x[n] = 6[(1/2)ⁿ − (1/3)ⁿ]u[n]. Causal; the ROC contains |z| = 1, so it is stable.

ROC |z| < 1/3: inside both poles, so both terms are left-sided: x[n] = −6(1/2)ⁿu[−n−1] + 6(1/3)ⁿu[−n−1] = 6[(1/3)ⁿ − (1/2)ⁿ]u[−n−1]. Values: x[−1] = 6(3 − 2) = 6, x[−2] = 6(9 − 4) = 30. Anti-causal, and it grows as n → −∞, so it is unstable; the ROC does not contain |z| = 1.

ROC 1/3 < |z| < 1/2: the pole at 1/3 is inside the ring (right-sided term) and the pole at 1/2 is outside (left-sided term): x[n] = −6(1/3)ⁿu[n] − 6(1/2)ⁿu[−n−1]. Values: x[0] = −6, x[1] = −2, x[−1] = −6 × 2 = −12, x[−2] = −24. Two-sided and unstable, because |z| = 1 is outside the ring.
Only |z| > 1/2 contains the unit circle, so only the causal answer is stable. A common slip is to call the middle ring stable: 1/3 < |z| < 1/2 lies entirely inside |z| = 1.

bank.q: A discrete-time LTI system obeys y[n] − 0.5y[n−1] = x[n]. Using the z-transform, find H(z), the impulse response, the pole-zero plot and the frequency response at ω = 0 and ω = π, and decide whether the causal system is stable.
outline: Transform with the shift rule, zero initial conditions
Pole at z = 0.5, zero at z = 0
Causal ROC |z| > 0.5 gives h[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n]
Pole inside the unit circle, so the causal system is stable
|H| = 2 at ω = 0 and 0.667 at ω = π: low-pass
answer: Take the z-transform of both sides with zero initial conditions. The shift rule gives y[n − 1] ↔ z<sup>−1</sup>Y(z), so Y(z) − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>Y(z) = X(z).
Transfer function: H(z) = Y(z)/X(z) = 1/(1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>). Multiply top and bottom by z: H(z) = z/(z − 0.5).

Poles and zeros: the denominator z − 0.5 = 0 gives one pole at z = 0.5; the numerator z = 0 gives one zero at the origin. On the plot, mark × at 0.5 on the real axis, ○ at 0, and draw the unit circle.
ROC: a causal system has an ROC outside its outermost pole, so ROC |z| > 0.5. Shade the region outside the circle of radius 0.5; the unit circle lies in it.
Impulse response: the pair z/(z − a) ↔ aⁿu[n] for |z| > |a| gives h[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n].

answer.text: Check by running the difference equation with x[n] = δ[n] and y[−1] = 0:

answer: Stability: Σ|h[n]| = 1 + 0.5 + 0.25 + … = 2, which is finite, so the system is BIBO stable. In pole terms, the causal system has its only pole at |z| = 0.5 < 1, inside the unit circle.
Frequency response: the ROC contains |z| = 1, so put z = e<sup>jω</sup>: H(e<sup>jω</sup>) = 1/(1 − 0.5e<sup>−jω</sup>), with |H(e<sup>jω</sup>)| = 1/√(1.25 − cos ω).

The gain falls from 2 at d.c. to 0.667 at ω = π, so the system is a low-pass filter. Geometrically, |H| is the distance from e<sup>jω</sup> to the zero divided by the distance to the pole; the point z = 1 is nearest the pole (distance 0.5), giving the largest gain 1/0.5 = 2.
Answer: H(z) = z/(z − 0.5), ROC |z| > 0.5; pole 0.5, zero 0; h[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n]; causal and stable; |H| = 2 at ω = 0 and 0.667 at ω = π.

bank.q: An LTI system has H(z) = (1 − z<sup>−1</sup>)/(1 − 0.9z<sup>−1</sup>) with ROC |z| > 0.9. Sketch |H(e<sup>jω</sup>)| over 0 ≤ ω ≤ π, mark its values at ω = 0, π/4, π/2 and π, and describe what the system does to a slowly varying input such as a daily temperature record.
outline: Zero at z = 1 blocks d.c.; pole at 0.9 lifts the response just above d.c.
High-pass (d.c. blocker) with a narrow notch at d.c.
Slow trends are removed; day-to-day changes pass
answer: Pole and zero: H(z) = (z − 1)/(z − 0.9). Zero at z = 1, which is the point ω = 0 on the unit circle; pole at z = 0.9, just inside the circle. The ROC |z| > 0.9 contains |z| = 1, so the causal system is stable and H(e<sup>jω</sup>) exists.
Frequency response: H(e<sup>jω</sup>) = (1 − e<sup>−jω</sup>)/(1 − 0.9e<sup>−jω</sup>).

answer.text: Magnitude squared, using |1 − ae<sup>−jω</sup>|² = 1 + a² − 2a cos ω:

answer: At ω = π the exact value is 2/1.9 = 1.0526. The curve is 0 at d.c., climbs steeply (already 0.725 at ω = 0.1 rad/sample), and is almost flat near 1.05 from about ω = 0.5 to π.
Sketch: horizontal axis ω from 0 to π, vertical axis |H| from 0 to 1.1. Start at 0, rise sharply, then run level just above 1 to ω = π. Mark the four computed points.

Why this shape: |H| equals (distance from e<sup>jω</sup> to the zero at 1) divided by (distance to the pole at 0.9). At ω = 0 the numerator is 0. As soon as e<sup>jω</sup> moves a little away from z = 1, both distances grow and become nearly equal, so the ratio settles near 1; at ω = π it is 2/1.9.
Character: a high-pass filter, more exactly a d.c. blocker with a narrow notch at ω = 0. Moving the pole nearer to 1 (say 0.99) narrows the notch further.

Effect on a daily temperature record (one sample per day): the long-term average and slow seasonal drift sit at frequencies near ω = 0, so they are removed or strongly reduced. Day-to-day changes sit at higher ω and pass with gain near 1.05. The output shows the departures from the recent level, not the level itself.

Check with a constant input x[n] = 25u[n] (a steady 25 °C): Y(z) = 25/(1 − z<sup>−1</sup>) · (1 − z<sup>−1</sup>)/(1 − 0.9z<sup>−1</sup>) = 25/(1 − 0.9z<sup>−1</sup>), so y[n] = 25(0.9)ⁿu[n] = 25, 22.5, 20.25, … The output starts at the jump and decays to 0, because the constant level is blocked.

bank.q: For H(z) = 1/(1 − 1.5z<sup>−1</sup> + 0.5z<sup>−2</sup>), find all possible ROCs, give the impulse response for each, and say which ROC gives a causal system and which gives a stable one.
outline: Factor: (1 − z<sup>−1</sup>)(1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>), poles at z = 1 and z = 0.5
Partial fractions: 2/(1 − z<sup>−1</sup>) − 1/(1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>)
|z| > 1 is causal; h[n] = (2 − 0.5ⁿ)u[n] is not summable
No ROC is stable, because a pole lies on the unit circle
answer: Factor the denominator: 1 − 1.5z<sup>−1</sup> + 0.5z<sup>−2</sup> = (1 − z<sup>−1</sup>)(1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>). Check: the product is 1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup> − z<sup>−1</sup> + 0.5z<sup>−2</sup>. Poles at z = 1 and z = 0.5.
Partial fractions: H(z) = A/(1 − z<sup>−1</sup>) + B/(1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>). Cover-up: A = 1/(1 − 0.5·1) = 1/0.5 = 2 (set z<sup>−1</sup> = 1); B = 1/(1 − 1·2) = −1 (set z<sup>−1</sup> = 2).
The ROC is bounded by the pole circles |z| = 0.5 and |z| = 1, so there are three choices.
ROC |z| > 1: both terms right-sided. h[n] = (2 − 0.5ⁿ)u[n] = 1, 1.5, 1.75, 1.875, … This is causal, but h[n] → 2, so Σ|h[n]| diverges: unstable.

ROC 0.5 < |z| < 1: the pole at 0.5 is inside (right-sided) and the pole at 1 is outside (left-sided). h[n] = −(0.5)ⁿu[n] − 2u[−n−1]: h[n] = −2 for every n ≤ −1 and −1, −0.5, −0.25, … for n ≥ 0. Two-sided, so not causal; Σ|h[n]| diverges because of the endless −2 values: unstable.
ROC |z| < 0.5: both terms left-sided. h[n] = −2u[−n−1] + (0.5)ⁿu[−n−1] = ((0.5)ⁿ − 2)u[−n−1]. Values: h[−1] = 2 − 2 = 0, h[−2] = 4 − 2 = 2, h[−3] = 6. Anti-causal and growing as n → −∞: unstable.
Why none is stable: stability needs an ROC that contains |z| = 1, and an ROC never contains a pole. A pole sits on the unit circle at z = 1, so no ROC can contain the whole circle.
Physical reading: the pole at z = 1 is an accumulator. The causal system adds up its input, so a step input gives an output that grows like 2n without bound, even though the input is bounded.

bank.q: Compare the DTFS, DTFT, DFT and z-transform in a table covering the class of signal each applies to and whether the description is discrete or continuous, finite or infinite, and periodic or not. Explain how each one is obtained from another, and check the links on numbers.
outline: DTFS: periodic sequence, N coefficients, periodic in k
DTFT: aperiodic sequence, continuous and 2π-periodic in ω
DFT: finite-length sequence, N values, implicitly periodic
z-transform: any sequence with a nonempty ROC, function of complex z
DTFT = X(z) on |z| = 1; DFT = DTFT sampled at 2πk/N; DTFS coefficients = DTFT of one period sampled at 2πk/N
Circular versus linear convolution

head: Transform
Applies to
Variable
Discrete or continuous
Finite or infinite
Periodic?
rows: yes, in k with period N
any x[n] with a nonempty ROC
no; the ROC is part of the answer

answer: z-transform to DTFT: put z = e<sup>jω</sup>. This is allowed only when the unit circle is in the ROC. Example: x[n] = (0.8)ⁿu[n] has X(z) = z/(z − 0.8), ROC |z| > 0.8; at z = 1 (ω = 0) it gives 1/0.2 = 5, the DTFT value at ω = 0.

DTFT to DFT: for a length-N sequence, X[k] = X(e<sup>jω</sup>) at ω = 2πk/N. Example: x = [1, 2, 3, 4] has DTFT 1 + 2e<sup>−jω</sup> + 3e<sup>−j2ω</sup> + 4e<sup>−j3ω</sup>; at ω = π/2 this is 1 − 2j − 3 + 4j = −2 + 2j, which is the 4-point DFT value X[1].

DTFT to DTFS: for a periodic sequence, the DTFS coefficient X[k] (with 1/N in synthesis) equals the DTFT of one period, sampled at ω = 2πk/N. Example: one period 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0 has period-DTFT 1 + e<sup>−jω</sup> + e<sup>−j2ω</sup>; at ω = 2π/8 this is 1 + (0.7071 − j0.7071) − j = 1.7071 − j1.7071 = X[1].

DFT and DTFS: the formulas are identical. The DFT of N samples is the DTFS of the periodic sequence made by repeating them. That is why every DFT operation is circular: shifts wrap modulo N, and multiplying DFTs gives circular convolution.

Circular versus linear: x = [1, 2, 3, 4] and h = [1, 1, 0, 0] give a 4-point circular convolution [5, 3, 5, 7], while the linear convolution is [1, 3, 5, 7, 4]; the last value 4 has wrapped onto n = 0 (1 + 4 = 5). Zero padding to 5 or more points makes the two agree.

Limits: keep one pulse fixed and let the period N of its periodic extension grow. The lines X[k] at 2πk/N crowd together and, with 1/N in synthesis, lie exactly on the DTFT curve of the pulse; in the limit the line spectrum becomes that curve. This is how the DTFT arises from the DTFS.

Which to use: DTFS for periodic sequences, DTFT for the exact spectrum of an aperiodic sequence, DFT for computation on a finite record (with an FFT), and the z-transform for systems, stability and difference equations, where the ROC carries causality and stability.

bank.q: A second-order causal system has poles at z = re<sup>±jθ</sup> with 0 < r < 1 and no finite zeros except at the origin. Derive its impulse response and frequency response, and discuss how r and θ set the decay rate, the ringing frequency and the resonant peak. Choose r and θ for a system that must ring at one-tenth of the sampling rate and fall below 1 % within fifty samples.
outline: H(z) = 1/(1 − 2r cos θ z<sup>−1</sup> + r²z<sup>−2</sup>)
h[n] = rⁿ sin((n + 1)θ)/sin θ · u[n]
r sets the decay rⁿ; θ sets the ringing frequency θ rad/sample
Peak near ω = θ, larger and narrower as r → 1
Stable for r < 1; at r = 1 it oscillates and is not BIBO stable
answer: Transfer function: with poles p = re<sup>jθ</sup> and p* = re<sup>−jθ</sup>, H(z) = 1/[(1 − pz<sup>−1</sup>)(1 − p*z<sup>−1</sup>)] = 1/(1 − 2r cos θ z<sup>−1</sup> + r²z<sup>−2</sup>), because p + p* = 2r cos θ and pp* = r². The difference equation is y[n] = 2r cos θ y[n−1] − r² y[n−2] + x[n].
Partial fractions: H(z) = A/(1 − pz<sup>−1</sup>) + A*/(1 − p*z<sup>−1</sup>) with A = p/(p − p*) = re<sup>jθ</sup>/(2jr sin θ) = e<sup>jθ</sup>/(2j sin θ).
Causal ROC |z| > r, so h[n] = (Apⁿ + A*p*ⁿ)u[n] = 2 Re{Apⁿ}u[n] = rⁿ · Re{e<sup>j(n+1)θ</sup>/(j sin θ)} · u[n] = rⁿ sin((n + 1)θ)/sin θ · u[n].
Reading the result: rⁿ is the envelope (decay set by r), and sin((n + 1)θ) is the ringing at θ rad/sample, a period of 2π/θ samples.

Frequency response: the ROC contains |z| = 1 when r < 1, so H(e<sup>jω</sup>) = 1/[(1 − re<sup>jθ</sup>e<sup>−jω</sup>)(1 − re<sup>−jθ</sup>e<sup>−jω</sup>)]. Near ω = θ the first factor has magnitude close to 1 − r, which is small, so |H| peaks near ω = θ. Its height grows roughly like 1/(1 − r), and its −3 dB width is roughly 2(1 − r) rad/sample.
Design for ringing: one-tenth of the sampling rate means one cycle every 10 samples, so θ = 2π/10 = 0.6283 rad/sample (36°).

Design for decay: the envelope must satisfy r<sup>50</sup> ≤ 0.01. So r ≤ 0.01<sup>1/50</sup> = e<sup>ln(0.01)/50</sup> = e<sup>−0.0921</sup> = 0.9120. Take r = 0.91, giving r<sup>50</sup> = 0.0090, under 1 %.
Coefficients: 2r cos θ = 2 × 0.91 × 0.8090 = 1.4724 and r² = 0.8281. The filter is y[n] = 1.4724y[n−1] − 0.8281y[n−2] + x[n].

answer.text: Check h[n] from the recursion against the closed form (sin θ = 0.5878):

answer: The zero crossings at n = 4 and n = 9 are 5 samples apart, half of the 10-sample period, as designed.

Peak of this design: computed |H(e<sup>jω</sup>)| has its maximum 9.90 at ω = 0.622 rad/sample, close to θ = 0.628; the gain at d.c. is 2.81 and at ω = π it is 0.303. The −3 dB width is 0.193 rad/sample, close to the estimate 2(1 − r) = 0.18.

Trade-off: r nearer 1 gives a taller, narrower peak and a longer ring (r = 0.99 would need about 460 samples to fall to 1 %); r smaller gives a quicker decay and a broad, low peak. θ moves the peak along the frequency axis without changing the decay.

Stability limits: for any r < 1 both poles are inside the unit circle and the causal system is BIBO stable. At r = 1 the poles sit on the circle: h[n] = sin((n + 1)θ)/sin θ never decays, Σ|h[n]| diverges, and the system is an oscillator, not BIBO stable. For r > 1 the ringing grows.

bank.q: You record 1024 samples of a machine vibration at 2048 samples per second and compute the DFT. Explain how record length, zero padding and windowing change what you see, and why two engineers using different record lengths may report different peak frequencies for the same machine. Use numbers.
outline: Bin spacing fₛ/N; the record lasts N/fₛ seconds
DFT bins are samples of the DTFT of the windowed record
Zero padding gives finer samples of the same curve, not finer resolution
Resolution about 1/T Hz is set by the record length and the window
Leakage from a rectangular window; tapering windows trade main-lobe width for lower sidelobes
A tone between bins shows at the nearest bin, so the reported peak depends on N
answer: Record: N = 1024 samples at fₛ = 2048 samples/s lasts T = N/fₛ = 0.5 s.
Bin spacing: the DFT gives X[k] at ω<sub>k</sub> = 2πk/N, which is f<sub>k</sub> = k·fₛ/N = k × 2 Hz. So the bins sit at 0, 2, 4, … Hz, up to the Nyquist frequency fₛ/2 = 1024 Hz at k = 512.

What a bin is: X[k] is a sample of the DTFT of the recorded block, that is, of the true spectrum seen through a 0.5 s rectangular window. The window turns each pure tone into a Dirichlet-shaped lobe whose main lobe reaches its first zeros 1/T = 2 Hz (one bin) on each side of the tone.

Resolution: two tones closer than about 1/T = 2 Hz merge into one lobe. Tones at 100 Hz and 101 Hz cannot be told apart in a 0.5 s record. A 1 s record (2048 samples) gives 1 Hz spacing and separates them.

Zero padding: appending 3072 zeros to make 4096 points gives bins every 0.5 Hz. These are new samples of the same lobe, so the peak position is read more finely, but 100 Hz and 101 Hz still merge, because the underlying curve has not changed.

Leakage: a tone that does not complete a whole number of cycles in the record ends with a jump when the DFT repeats the block, so energy spreads into many bins. With the rectangular window the first sidelobe is only about 13 dB below the peak, so a weak tone next to a strong one can be hidden.

Windowing: tapering the record (for example with a Hann window) lowers the sidelobes to about 31 dB below the peak, so weak tones appear, but the main lobe doubles in width (about ±4 Hz here), which worsens resolution. The choice is a trade-off between seeing weak tones and separating close ones.

answer.text: Why two engineers disagree: suppose the machine runs at 50.7 Hz.

answer: Both readings are honest samples of the same spectrum, one at a 2 Hz grid and one at a 1 Hz grid. Neither equals 50.7 Hz. Engineer A could get closer by zero padding to 4096 points (bins at 50.5 and 51.0 Hz; the peak would show at 50.5 Hz, 0.2 Hz away) or by interpolating between the two largest bins.

Good practice: state fₛ, N, the window and any zero padding with every reported spectrum; choose the record length from the resolution needed (T ≥ 1/Δf); use a window when weak tones matter; and interpolate the peak rather than quoting the largest bin.

bank.q: Explain deconvolution with the z-transform. Given Y(z) = H(z)X(z), discuss when the inverse system 1/H(z) is causal and stable, illustrate with H(z) = (1 − 2z<sup>−1</sup>)/(1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>), and say what happens when H(z) has a zero on the unit circle.
outline: Inverse system H<sub>i</sub>(z) = 1/H(z); its poles are the zeros of H
Causal and stable inverse needs every zero of H inside the unit circle (minimum phase)
Zero at 2: causal inverse unstable; a stable inverse exists only if non-causal
Zero on the circle: inverse has a pole on the circle, infinite gain there
Noise is amplified where |H| is small
answer: Deconvolution means recovering x[n] from y[n] = h[n] * x[n] when h[n] is known. In the z-domain Y(z) = H(z)X(z), so X(z) = Y(z)/H(z): pass y[n] through the inverse system H<sub>i</sub>(z) = 1/H(z). Examples are channel equalisation and removing an echo.
Poles and zeros swap: the zeros of H(z) become the poles of H<sub>i</sub>(z), and the poles of H become its zeros. So the stability of the inverse depends on the zeros of H, not on its poles.

Rule: a causal inverse has ROC outside its outermost pole, so it is stable only if every pole of H<sub>i</sub>, that is every zero of H, lies strictly inside the unit circle. A causal, stable H whose zeros are all inside the circle is called minimum phase, and only such a system has a causal, stable inverse.
The example: H(z) = (1 − 2z<sup>−1</sup>)/(1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>) has its pole at 0.5 (H is causal and stable) and its zero at 2 (outside the circle). So H is not minimum phase.

Inverse: H<sub>i</sub>(z) = (1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>)/(1 − 2z<sup>−1</sup>), with a pole at 2 and a zero at 0.5. Split it: H<sub>i</sub>(z) = 0.25 + 0.75/(1 − 2z<sup>−1</sup>). Check: 0.25(1 − 2z<sup>−1</sup>) + 0.75 = 1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>.
Causal choice, ROC |z| > 2: h<sub>i</sub>[n] = 0.25δ[n] + 0.75·2ⁿu[n] = 1, 1.5, 3, 6, … This grows without bound, so the causal inverse is unstable.

Stable choice, ROC |z| < 2 (it contains |z| = 1): h<sub>i</sub>[n] = 0.25δ[n] − 0.75·2ⁿu[−n−1]. Values: h<sub>i</sub>[0] = 0.25, h<sub>i</sub>[−1] = −0.375, h<sub>i</sub>[−2] = −0.1875, … Σ|h<sub>i</sub>| = 0.25 + 0.75(1/2 + 1/4 + …) = 0.25 + 0.75 = 1, finite, so it is stable but non-causal: it needs future samples of y[n]. In practice this is done on stored data, or approximated with a delay.

Minimum-phase contrast: H(z) = 1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup> has its zero at 0.5, and 1/H(z) = 1/(1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>) with |z| > 0.5 gives h<sub>i</sub>[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n], causal and stable. Check: (1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>)·1/(1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>) = 1, so h * h<sub>i</sub> = δ[n].

Zero on the unit circle: H(z) = 1 − z<sup>−1</sup> (a first difference) has |H(e<sup>j0</sup>)| = 0. Its inverse 1/(1 − z<sup>−1</sup>) is an accumulator with a pole at z = 1, not BIBO stable, and its gain at d.c. is infinite: the d.c. part of x[n] was wiped out by H and cannot be recovered.

Noise: if y[n] carries noise, the inverse multiplies it by 1/|H(e<sup>jω</sup>)|; where |H| = 0.1 the noise grows ten times. For the example H, |H| = |1 − 2|/|1 − 0.5| = 2 at ω = 0 and |1 + 2|/|1 + 0.5| = 2 at ω = π; in fact |H| = 2 at every ω (H is an all-pass filter times 2), so its stable inverse has gain 0.5 everywhere and does not boost noise. The difficulty with this H is causality, not noise.

Conclusion: deconvolution is exact and stable in real time only for minimum-phase H; zeros outside the circle force a non-causal inverse, and zeros on or near the circle make the inverse blow up or amplify noise, which is why practical equalisers limit their gain.

glossary.def: The representation of a periodic discrete-time sequence as a finite sum of N complex exponentials.
The representation of an aperiodic sequence as a continuous, 2π-periodic function of frequency ω.
An N-point transform that maps N time samples to N frequency samples equally spaced over one full 2π turn.
The power series X(z) = Σ x[n] z<sup>−n</sup> that generalises the DTFT to complex values of z.
The set of complex z values for which the z-transform sum converges absolutely.
A value of z at which the transfer function or transform becomes infinite.
A value of z at which the numerator, and hence the transform, equals zero.
The set |z| = 1 in the z-plane; on it the z-transform becomes the DTFT.
The constant W<sub>N</sub> = e<sup>−j2π/N</sup> raised to integer powers inside the DFT sum.
The N-point convolution in which indices wrap modulo N; it is what multiplying two N-point DFTs gives.
The ordinary convolution sum of two aperiodic sequences, equal to circular convolution when the period is long enough.
A sequence that is zero for all negative values of n.
A sequence that is zero for every n below some finite index n₀ (n₀ may be negative).
Property that the sum of the magnitudes of the sequence terms is finite.
A way of writing a rational transform as a sum of simple fractions whose inverse transforms are known.
The z-transform of the impulse response of an LTI system; it equals Y(z)/X(z) for zero initial conditions.
The complex gain H(e<sup>jω</sup>) that an LTI system applies to a complex exponential input at frequency ω.
A relation expressing the present output sample in terms of past outputs and present and past inputs.
The property that every bounded input produces a bounded output; for a causal system it means all poles of H(z) lie inside the unit circle.
A causal, stable system whose zeros also all lie inside the unit circle, so a causal stable inverse exists.
The spreading of energy from one frequency bin into neighbouring bins when the record length is not an integer number of periods.
Appending zeros to a finite record before the DFT, which interpolates the spectrum without improving resolution.
Inverting X(z) by dividing numerator by denominator; the coefficient of z<sup>−n</sup> is x[n] for a right-sided sequence.
